Add a numerical stable implementation of the logit function, the inverse of the sigmoid function, and its derivative.
y = ln(x/(1-x))

It should be as easy to use the inverse of the sigmoid as it is to use the sigmoid function without having to worry about a numerical stable implementation.

Pitch
Add torch.logit.

Alternatives
A current version of the logit could look like this:
y = torch.log(x) - torch.log1p(-x)

Currently, DDP creates buckets to consolidate gradient communications. This helps to reduce the total communication delay, but increases the memory footprint. We can potentially let DDP set param.grad to point to different offsets in the bucket, so that AccumulateGrad can update grads in place. In this way, we can avoid two copies of grads and at the same time avoid conducting copy operations to and from the bucket.

🐛 Bug
Under ceil_mode=True for AvgPooling2d, Pytorch fails in calculating pooling output shape as expected, and gets NaN results, no matter executing with CPU version or GPU version.
Taking Pytorch with CPU version as an example, given an input with the shape (1, 16, 4, 4), I get an unexpected output under layer the AvgPool2d , which contains NaN(Not a Number) results，as shown in the following picture.

In this case, the parameters of AvgPool2d are as follows:
{
  'kernel_size': (1, 2), 
 'padding': (0, 1), 
 'stride': (2, 2),
 'ceil_mode': True, 
 'count_include_pad': True}
To investigate the root cause of such NaN results, I conduct a code tracing in the source code of Pytorch when executing AvgPool2d. Relevant code can be found inaten/src/ATen/native/Pool.h  and aten/src/ATen/native/AveragePool2d.cpp.
Firstly, Pytorch invokes the function pooling_output_shape_pad_lr in aten/src/ATen/native/AveragePool2d.cpp line 129-130  to calculate to pooling output shape.

Then Pytorch passes the two parameters outputHeight and outputWidth to function avg_pool2d_out_frame in aten/src/ATen/native/AveragePool2d.cpp (near line 14) to calculate the average pooling for each pool unit.
The implementation of pooling_output_shape_pad_lr is defined in aten/src/ATen/native/Pool.h (near line 25) . See the following picture.

The parameter ceil_mode=True indicates Pytorch uses ceil value instead of floor value when getting an output (refer to the official  website). For pooling calculations,  the ceil_mode=True may make the last pool unit start outside the image. From the above code, we know that Pytorch tries to avoid such condition  by executing --outputsize. This indeed works, but is only be triggered when using padding on this dimension (seeif(pad_l) line 31). In other words, if there is no padding  (pad_l=0) on this dimension, the outputsize will not be reduced by 1.
As a result, passing the output shape (also called out-of-range output shape) to avg_pool2d_out_frame, it will cause the last pool unit to be outside the image, as shown in the following example.

To be specific, an out-of-range output shape will generate a hstart(or wstart) whose value is greater or equal to hend（or wend), thus making the pool_size=(hend-hstart)*(wstart-wend) be zero or a negative value,  as shown between the line 46-83 in  aten/src/ATen/native/AveragePool2d.cpp.

In particular, just as our example, when hstart=hend (or wstart=wend ), it will make poolsize = 0,divide_factor=0 andsum = 0. Consequently,  the corresponding average pooling unit is calculated with  0 divided by 0, thus triggering NaN. Actually, the premise of function avg_pool2d_out_frame is that hstart  and wstart  are always smaller than hend and wend, and this needs to be guaranteed by the previous function pooling_output_shape_pad_lr in pool.h. But due to if (pad_l), it only executes the relevant judgments and reductions when using padding on this dimension.
In addition, I also try multiple sets of other different parameters. They all trigger the NaN problem
on both CPU and GPU version, because of the same reason (hstart=hend), as shown in the following table.



Parameters for AvgPool2D
Input Shape
Output Shape




{'ceil_mode': True, 'count_include_pad': True, 'kernel_size': (1, 4), 'padding': (0, 1), 'stride': (2, 2)}
(1, 16, 32, 32)
(1, 16, 17, 16)


{'ceil_mode': True, 'count_include_pad': True, 'kernel_size': 2, 'padding': (0, 1), 'stride': (3, 3)}
(1, 16, 9, 9)
(1, 16, 4, 4)


{'ceil_mode': True, 'count_include_pad': True, 'kernel_size': (1, 3), 'padding': (0, 1), 'stride': (4, 4)}
（1,16,4,4）
(1, 16, 2, 2)



Key insight
Under the ceil_mode=True, the statement if (pad_l)  in function pooling_output_shape_pad_lr (see aten/src/ATen/native/Pool.h ) cannot reduce the out-of-range outputshape, making some pools are taken outside the input image.  Such situations occur in both CPU version and GPU version. Even worse, the special case when hstart=hend or wstart=wend will trigger the NaN output. Such NaN output in pooling operations will confuse users, and also will affect the subsequent calculation in the model, causing unexpected results.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Just run the following code.

Code to reproduce
import numpy as np
import torch
   
kwargs = {
	'ceil_mode': True, 
	'count_include_pad': True, 
	'kernel_size': (1, 2), 
	'padding': (0, 1), 
	'stride': (2, 2)
	}  
input = (10 * np.random.randn(1,16,4,4)).astype(np.float32)    
layer = torch.nn.AvgPool2d(**kwargs)
modelinput=torch.from_numpy(input)
output = layer(modelinput)
ytrue=output.detach().numpy()
nanresult=np.isnan(ytrue).any()

print(nanresult)

Expected behavior
The output is a matrix of constants, at least no 'Nan'

nodes.bodyText:
A common situation when reporting errors is that we don't know enough about the context at the point we are reporting the error. For example, in the new op registration API we have:
#define DEF_PRELUDE "def(\"", schema.operator_name(), "\"): "
Library& Library::_def(c10::FunctionSchema&& schema, c10::OperatorName* out_name) & {
  TORCH_CHECK(kind_ == DEF || kind_ == FRAGMENT,
    DEF_PRELUDE,
    "Cannot define an operator inside of a ", kind_, " block.  "
    "All def()s should be placed in the (unique) TORCH_LIBRARY block for their namespace.  ",
    ERROR_CONTEXT
  );

However, the description of what the shape of the def operation was is misleading, because _def may be called from the implementation of def(schema, impl) (and so the error message would misreport that it's from a def(schema) call). These things may seem minor, but there are more major situations where lack of context can seriously impede understanding of an error message (e.g., a BLAS failure in some low level helper function, which should we report as having occurred when someone did a matrix multiply call.)
Today, c10::Error supports a limited form of error context in the form of its AppendMessage method, which can be used append an arbitrary string at the end of the existing c10 exception string. This is used in very few places. The purpose of this issue is to propose a more general formatting and API convention for adding context, with the intent of using it more broadly in the codebase.

Typical message format today:
>>> torch.zeros(2,3) + torch.zeros(3,2)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
RuntimeError: The size of tensor a (3) must match the size of tensor b (2) at non-singleton dimension 1

Suggested updated format with context:
>>> torch.zeros(2,3) + torch.zeros(3,2)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
RuntimeError: The size of tensor a (3) must match the size of tensor b (2) at non-singleton dimension 1
  In operator "add.Tensor"

Notes about format:

Each line of context is indented two spaces and occupies a newline. (The expectation is that context is short and does not need to line wrap). Context is capitalized. Unless you have a good reason not to, it should start with "In ..."
Lines of context do NOT record the C++ file/line number that installed them (But perhaps in a hypothetical mode where we unconditionally report C++ backtraces, c.f. #25716, we could also contain file and line numbers of the context adding lines)

EDIT: I have a suggested refinement on format. If there is only one line of error context, we should fold it into the previous line. So you have:
RuntimeError: The size of tensor a (3) must match the size of tensor b (2) at non-singleton dimension 1 (In operator "add.Tensor")

With two lines, we give them separate lines:
RuntimeError: The size of tensor a (3) must match the size of tensor b (2) at non-singleton dimension 1
  In operator "add.Tensor"
  In operator "addmm"

How to augment errors in this way, from C++:
try {
  ...
} catch (c10::Error& e) {
  TORCH_RERAISE(e, "Context message");
}

Context message follows the same formatting conventions as TORCH_CHECK.
Possible alternatives:

Install context as "fake" C++ frames in the Python backtrace. We shouldn't do this as it may interfere with IDE support of jump to error (which will only expect Python files in the trace)
Use TorchScript style error reporting. TorchScript style errors look like:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test.py", line 10, in <module>
    print(scripted_f("0_1"))
RuntimeError: The following operation failed in the TorchScript interpreter.
Traceback of TorchScript (most recent call last):
  File "test.py", line 6, in parse_float_from_str
def parse_float_from_str(s: str) -> float:
    return float(torch.split(s, "_", -1)[0])
           ~~~~~ <--- HERE
RuntimeError: Only 'inf' or '-inf' can be cast to a float, but got '0'

I'd prefer not to use this style because having two tracebacks in the error message impedes understanding of the error block; most PyTorch errors should just have one "Traceback", and the error context I'm thinking of would apply to most PyTorch errors

Print the entire C++ stack trace. This is generally not so useful to end users; while they can crack open the Python code referenced by a Python backtrace, there is generally no way to get to the C++ code (or modify it and see what happens)

I think backprop through torch.where is wrong in certain special cases.
To Reproduce
t = 0
x = torch.ones(()).requires_grad_()
y = t * (x / t)  # just an example; anything that produces nan's works
z = torch.where(x >= t, x, y)
z.backward()

# the forward pass works fine (the `nan`'s in `y` do not affect z)
# NOTE: this is unlike a naive implement of where that does `cond * x + (1 - cond) * y`
print(z)
# tensor(1., grad_fn=<SWhereBackward>)

# but the backward pass backprops the `nan`'s from y into x, even though the y path is never taken in torch.where
print(x.grad)
# tensor(nan)
Expected behavior
print(x.grad)
# tensor(1.)
This would be the correct gradient.
In practice, this bug can easily happen if one runs the above code for different t (including 0) and assumes that the nan's for t = 0 should not matter because the torch.where always selects the first path that has no nans (and the forward pass does handle it correctly).
Environment

PyTorch Version 1.4

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 Feature

I'd like to propose a new feature of the torch.utils.data.DataLoaderclass, to have its batch_size equal to len(dataset)
Motivation
Sometimes when testing and/or validating my model, I want to change the ratio of training set to the test/val set. When I do testing, though, I frequently wish to not have more than one iteration, but pass the entire dataset at once. I usually just bypass this with batch_size=len(dataset), but that seems very inelegant to me.
Even more worrying situation is, when cross validating, to have data splits with different sizes. Although that too can me mitigated, in this case by dropping data, why not allow users not to drop it?

Pitch
# Let's load our test set
test_loader = DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size=.....
# Wait I forgot what the dimensions are... Ah how frustrating
# Oh well I could use len() I guess
test_loader = DataLoader(test_dataset, batch_size=len(test_dataset))
# Well that looks just plain ugly. I wish there was a better way...

Alternatives
As I said, the alternatives are either changing the batch sizes manually for every dataloader when testing/validating, or using the inelegant len(dataset) or even .shape attribute of tensors.

Possible implementations
It could be implemented by setting batch_size to 0 or -1.
Additional context
As I'm a student, most of my datasets are either The Standard Ones or very small real world datasets that can store entire test/val datasets in memory, but I do see that there definitely exist use cases where it is impossible to store test sets in memory at once.
Also, I'm also kinda looking to start contributing to open source and I figured this would be the best way I guess.

cc @ssnl

It's common to use assertion to check pre-conditions or unexpected inputs in code, as a form of defensive programming. For example, sometimes we want to assert that all elements of a tensor is all positive, or finite.

when dealing with cuda tensors, using python's assert (t>0).all() or assert torch.isfinite(t).all() will wait for results of the cuda kernel and most if not all its preceding kernel launches, thus potentially cause significantly slow down.
It would be good to have a way to execute an assert as an async call.
it does not work nicely with tracing or FX, because it is considered as control logic

Pitch
x = some_tensor()
(x>0).all().assert("I got a bad data x")
y = torch.log(x)
torch.Assert(y.all(), "message")

(assert is a reserved keyword. Tensorflow uses tf.Assert. we can also use torch.assert_ since the op can be used with in-place style: y.all().assert_())
cc @ngimel

@lw and @jiayisuse brought up a great point that RPC system should work correctly even if the agent only uses a single thread to process all internal messages. Otherwise, the correctness of RPC will depend on the thread number configuration, which is not ideal. Currently, if ProcessGroupAgent catches an exception in its listenLoop, it prevents any further sends/receives from the agent, but it also doesn't shutdown. This leaves the agent in somewhat of a "zombie" state - it can do nothing and must wait for its shutdown function to be called.
One possible exception PGA may encounter is the "connection closed by peer" error seen when another agent shuts down during communication. For elasticity to work in the future, we cannot have all agents in the gang enter a dysfunctional state if only one shutdown. Additionally, in order for test_backward_node_failure_python_udf to succeed, we must allow agents to continue receiving and processing messages (or shutdown) even if another agent shuts down.
Thus we must do one of the following if PGA encounters an exception in listenLoop:

Shutdown the Agent. This should make test_backward_node_failure_python_udf pass, and is still logical right now given that we have no elasticity guarantees around the RPC framework currently. In essence, if one agent shuts down, they all shut down.
Continue allowing send/recv. This will make the test pass and enable elasticity going forward. If the Tensorpipe RPC Agent becomes the go-to RPC backend by the time elasticity in the RPC framework is shipped, a simple shutdown should suffice.

cc @pietern @mrshenli @pritamdamania87 @zhaojuanmao @satgera @rohan-varma @gqchen @aazzolini @xush6528 @osalpekar @jjlilley

TracedModuel currently returns the compiled code via the .code() member function. This code can possible contain constants (e.g. CONSTANTS.c0), however the value of these are not accessible from python at the moment. It would really useful to surface the constant mapping to python so libraries that interpret the module can get the full picture.

I am currently writing a pytorch/torchscript -> mxnet code converter and currently it cannot resolve the constants in the torchscript code.
Pitch
tracedmodule.code -> returns code (done)
tracedmoduel.constants -> returns a mapping between constant name and value (dict)
Alternatives
Any other function from jit that can return the constants of a tracedmodule
Additional context

🐛 Bug
Calling from_dlpack in another process before cuda.is_initialized() on an CUDA IPC handle results in RuntimeError: CUDA error: invalid argument (seems to be coming from at::fromDLPack). Note that allocating a dummy cuda tensor (e.g. torch.ones) first to start lazy initialization makes from_dlpack work.
To Reproduce
Here is a code snippet to reproduce the result. I tried to minimize the steps involved but requires cupy and pycuda. Notice the comment that can trigger it to work. IPC packing/unpacking seems to work for cupy, torch has the issue.
#!/usr/bin/env python

import multiprocessing as mp

def worker(ipc_ptr, shape, dtype):
    import pycuda.driver as cuda
    import pycuda.autoinit
    import cupy
    from torch.utils import dlpack
    import torch
    # dummy_init = torch.ones(1, device=torch.device("cuda")) # uncomment to make it work as expected
    data_ptr = cuda.IPCMemoryHandle(ipc_ptr)
    buff = {'data': (int(data_ptr), False), 'shape': shape, 'typestr': dtype}
    class capsule(object):
        pass
    cap = capsule()
    cap.__cuda_array_interface__ = buff
    cuarray = cupy.asanyarray(cap)
    print("cupy array from IPC", cuarray.shape)
    pack = cuarray.toDlpack()
    cuarray2 = cupy.fromDlpack(pack)
    print("cupy array from DLPack", cuarray2.shape)
    pack2 = cuarray2.toDlpack()
    tensor = dlpack.from_dlpack(pack2)
    print("Pytorch Tensor from_dlpack", tensor.shape)

def pytorch_ipc_dlpack():
    import pycuda.driver as cuda
    import pycuda.autoinit
    import cupy
    tensor = cupy.ones([1, 2, 3])
    ipc_ptr = cuda.mem_get_ipc_handle(tensor.data.ptr)
    shape = tensor.shape
    dtype = str(tensor.dtype)
    proc = mp.Process(target=worker, args=(ipc_ptr, shape, dtype))
    proc.start()
    proc.join()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mp.set_start_method("spawn")
    pytorch_ipc_dlpack()
Expected behavior
I expect from_dlpack to handle lazy initialization correctly.
